newsitem.title: UK: Sports don't make teens behave, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Sports don't make teens behave, study finds.

text.p: Playing sports does not stop lively boys and girls from becoming juvenile delinquents, and could make them worse, New Zealand researchers reported on Thursday.
Dr Dorathy Begg and colleagues at the University of Otago medical school in Dunedin questioned more than 1,000 boys and girls aged 15 to 18, asking them about sports and delinquent activity.
Delinquency was defined by 29 different acts, including car theft, burglary and shoplifting. Sport included just about everything from aerobics to windsurfing.

They found that boys who did a lot of sport by the age of 15 were twice as likely to be delinquent by 18 as boys who were not athletic in their early teens. Athletic girls were nearly three times as likely to misbehave.

"It is considered that "sport builds character' and that participating in organised sport, young people are exposed to strong conforming, rather than deviant, influences," they wrote in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.
But team sports seemed to be excluded from the effect.

"Conventional sports which incorporate many aspects of the broader society (for example rules, regulations, authority figures) may appeal to the non-delinquent, but for the delinquent, who by definition violates the rules and norms of society, these activities offer little appeal," they concluded.
